Juvenile fire clownfish (Amphiprion melanopus) typically attain sexual maturity at a relatively modest size, with puberty commencing once individuals reach a standard length of approximately 5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 5 centimeters]. This developmental milestone is accompanied by a concurrent increase in somatic mass, with the corresponding wet weight at puberty averaging around 2.9 grams [Wwp = around 2.9 grams]. These values were derived from a long-term mark-recapture study conducted on the reef slopes of Papua New Guinea, where individual growth trajectories were monitored over several consecutive spawning seasons. In contrast to many other pomacentrids inhabiting similar coral reef habitats, the relatively small body size at maturity in this species likely reflects the selective pressures of living within the confines of a host sea anemone, where spatial limitations may constrain overall growth potential. Continued growth proceeds steadily after the onset of reproductive capability, and fully grown adults ultimately reach a maximum standard length of approximately 12 centimeters [Li = approximately 12 centimeters].

The wet weight trajectory of Amphiprion melanopus follows a predictable allometric relationship with standard length, and comprehensive sampling of adult individuals from the population revealed that the ultimate wet weight, or maximum recorded adult body mass, is approximately 41.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 41.5 grams]. This species exhibits a moderately rapid early growth phase, with newly hatched larvae measuring a mere 0.0037 grams [Wwb = 0.0037 grams] in wet weight at the moment of emergence from the egg. This remarkably low birth mass, equivalent to roughly 0.0037 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.0037 grams], is consistent with the small egg size characteristic of the genus. The eggs themselves measure between 3.0 and 3.3 millimeters in length and 1.1 to 1.9 millimeters in width, and the calculated neonatal mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to support the larva through its initial endotrophic phase prior to the onset of exogenous feeding.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C], the embryonic development of Amphiprion melanopus proceeds rapidly, and the age at birth, defined as the time from oviposition to the hatching of the yolk-sac larva, is approximately 7.5 days [ab = approximately 7.5 days]. Following eclosion, the prolarvae remain lecithotrophic for a brief period, with complete yolk-sac resorption occurring roughly 7 hours after hatching. These developmental parameters were recorded during a captive breeding program in which water quality and thermal conditions were carefully regulated to mimic the stable environment of a tropical reef flat. The speed of embryonic development observed is broadly consistent with reports for other anemonefish species, although subtle interspecific variation in hatching time has been noted in the literature. The thermal sensitivity of early life stages is particularly pronounced in this lineage, as even minor deviations from the optimal temperature range can significantly alter the duration of embryonic development.

Reproductive output in the fire clownfish is tightly linked to the social structure of the group, with the dominant breeding female producing multiple clutches throughout the extended spawning season. Under optimal thermal conditions at 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C], field observations indicate that females lay clutches of approximately 20 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 20 eggs per spawning event], with approximately 19.7 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 19.7 spawning events per year]. Smaller, subordinate females within the group typically exhibit reduced fecundity and longer inter-spawning intervals, a pattern driven by the hormonal suppression mediated by the dominant pair.

The maximum documented lifespan for Amphiprion melanopus under natural reef conditions, derived from long-term photographic identification records of individually recognizable fish, is approximately 11 years [am = approximately 11 years] at a temperature of 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C]. This longevity is relatively substantial for a fish of this body size and is comparable to the lifespans reported for other anemonefish species that share a similar mutualistic lifestyle. The extended lifespan is thought to be a consequence of the elevated survivorship afforded by living in association with a venomous host anemone, which provides effective refuge from a wide array of piscine predators. Older individuals, particularly those that have transitioned from the non-reproductive subordinate state to become the dominant female, often display a gradual decline in reproductive output during their final years of life, though senescence-related mortality typically occurs only after the fish has exceeded 4000 days of age.
